Abstract. Methods and algorithms that work with data on nonlinear manifolds are collectively
5
summarized under the term ‘Riemannian computing’. In practice, curvature can be a key limiting
6
factor for the performance of Riemannian computing methods. Yet, curvature can also be a powerful
7
tool in the theoretical analysis of Riemannian algorithms. In this work, we investigate the sectional
8
curvature of the Stiefel and Grassmann manifold. On the Grassmannian, tight curvature bounds are
9
known since the late 1960ies. On the Stiefel manifold under the canonical metric, it was believed
10
that the sectional curvature does not exceed 5/4. Under the Euclidean metric, the maximum was
11
conjectured to be at 1. For both manifolds, the sectional curvature is given by the Frobenius norm of
12
certain structured commutator brackets of skew-symmetric matrices. We provide refined inequalities
13
for such terms and pay special attention to the maximizers of the curvature bounds. In this way,
14
we prove for the Stiefel manifold that the global bounds of 5/4 (canonical metric) and 1 (Euclidean
15
metric) hold indeed. With this addition, a complete account of the curvature bounds in all admissible
16
dimensions is obtained. We observe that ‘high curvature means low-rank’, more precisely, for the
17
Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds under the canonical metric, the global curvature maximum is
18
attained at tangent plane sections that are spanned by rank-two matrices, while the extreme curvature
19
cases of the Euclidean Stiefel manifold occur for rank-one matrices. Numerical examples are included
20
for illustration purposes.

1. Introduction. Methods and algorithms that work with data on nonlinear
25
Riemannian manifolds are collectively summarised under the term Riemannian com-
26
puting. Riemannian computing methods have established themselves as important
27
tools in a large variety of applications, including computer vision, machine learning,
28
and optimization, see [1, 2, 5, 9, 11, 19, 25, 26] and the anthologies [20, 27]. They also
29

30

31
A standard technique in designing Riemannian computing methods is to translate
32
Euclidean algorithms to manifolds. The discrepancy between a linear space and a
33
non-linear manifold is quantified by the concept of curvature. Therefore, curvature
34
can also be seen as a decisive factor that separates Riemannian algorithms from their
35
Euclidean counterparts. On the other hand, curvature estimates allow to compare
36
Euclidean distances and Riemannian distances for embedded submanifolds [4], which
37
can be a powerful tool in the theoretical analysis of Riemannian methods.
38

39
manifolds.

40
before. On the Grassmannian, tight curvature bounds are known since the seminal
41
papers of Wong [30, 31]. The sectional curvature on the Stiefel manifold under a
42
parametric family of Riemannian metrics introduced in [15] was extensively studied
43
in [21].

Abstract: Methods and algorithms that work with data on nonlinear manifolds are collectively 5 summarized under the term ‘Riemannian computing’. In practice, curvature can be a key limiting 6 factor for the performance of Riemannian computing methods. Yet, curvature can also be a powerful 7 tool in the theoretical analysis of Riemannian algorithms. In this work, we investigate the sectional 8 curvature of the Stiefel and Grassmann manifold. On the Grassmannian, tight curvature bounds are 9 known since the late 1960ies. On the Stiefel manifold under the canonical metric, it was believed 10 that the sectional curvature does not exceed 5/4. Under the Euclidean metric, the maximum was 11 conjectured to be at 1. For both manifolds, the sectional curvature is given by the Frobenius norm of 12 certain structured commutator brackets of skew-symmetric matrices. We provide refined inequalities 13 for such terms and pay special attention to the maximizers of the curvature bounds. In this way, 14 we prove for the Stiefel manifold that the global bounds of 5/4 (canonical metric) and 1 (Euclidean 15 metric) hold indeed. With this addition, a complete account of the curvature bounds in all admissible 16 dimensions is obtained. We observe that ‘high curvature means low-rank’, more precisely, for the 17 Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds under the canonical metric, the global curvature maximum is 18 attained at tangent plane sections that are spanned by rank-two matrices, while the extreme curvature 19 cases of the Euclidean Stiefel manifold occur for rank-one matrices. Numerical examples are included 20 for illustration purposes. 21
